topic: Evidence on time-restricted eating (intermittent fasting) versus continuous calorie restriction for weight loss and metabolic health

key_points.point: A 2026 Cochrane review (22 RCTs, 1,995 adults) found intermittent fasting no better than regular dietary advice such as continuous restriction: weight difference -0.33% (95% CI -0.92 to 0.26), low certainty.

The 12-month NEJM trial (139 adults) found calorie restriction plus 8am-4pm eating gave -8.0 kg versus -6.3 kg with calorie restriction alone, a non-significant difference; calorie deficit drove most benefit.
Lowe et al. (JAMA Intern Med 2020, 116 adults, 12 weeks) found 16:8 TRE did not beat consistent three-meal timing for weight (between-group -0.26 kg, P=.63) or most metabolic markers.

An umbrella review/network meta-analysis (BMC Med 2024; 153 studies, 9,846 people) found direct TRE vs continuous energy restriction weight difference -2.41 kg (CI -5.14 to 0.33), non-significant; most direct evidence was low or very low quality.

A JAMA Netw Open 2024 meta-analysis (29 RCTs, 2,485 adults, 12+ weeks) found TRE lowered weight by 1.37 kg (CI -1.99 to -0.75) versus controls; authors called this small, of uncertain clinical importance, and low certainty.

Energy intake reduction is the main driver: TRE trials show about 164 kcal/day lower intake, and a Nutrition Reviews meta-analysis found larger weight effects vs non-isocaloric controls (-2.82 kg) than isocaloric ones (-1.46 kg).

Metabolic benefits of TRE are modest: fasting glucose about -1.15 mg/dL and HbA1c -0.08% vs controls, with no significant change in LDL or blood pressure; TRE added to calorie restriction gave no extra BP, glucose or lipid benefit.
Adding TRE to calorie restriction gave a small extra weight reduction of about 1.4 kg (WMD -1.40, 95% CI -1.81 to -1.00; 8 trials, 579 adults) with low or very low certainty.
Lean mass is a concern: pooled TRE trials show about 0.42 kg lean mass loss, and Lowe et al. found a greater appendicular lean mass index decrease with TRE than with regular meal timing.

Versus no intervention, intermittent fasting gave -3.42% weight change (moderate certainty), but Cochrane authors judged this unlikely to be clinically meaningful; safety and quality-of-life data were sparse and inconsistently reported.

Evidence limits: trials are short (mostly under 12-16 months), small, heterogeneous in eating windows, often high risk of bias, and unrepresentative (NEJM trial mean age about 32); long-term sustainability and hard outcomes are unproven.
